**Title:** Which Dollar Broke? Separating Token Failures from Platform-Ledger Failures in Web Dollar Markets

**Abstract (273 words):**

Crypto prices on the Web are quoted in two kinds of dollar: stablecoin tokens, and balances in an exchange's internal ledger that reach the banking system only through the platform's rails. When a dollar price dislocates, either the token or the ledger has failed. The answer matters to users, price feeds and oracles, and we know of no measure that separates the two. The difficulty is that a ledger's value is never quoted directly, public prices are asynchronous last trades that thin out under stress, and any single asset may carry its own shock. We price the platform's dollar through an unpegged asset (BTC) against a venue whose rails stay open, which splits any dollar-quoted dislocation into a token and a ledger component, and we require unrelated assets to agree and the venue's internal cross-rates to hold. On Binance.US the method attributes all but 6% of the USDC dislocation in the March 2023 bank run to the token, and 99% of the June–July 2023 dislocation to the platform's dollar after its banks withdrew: that dollar traded at a discount while withdrawals were threatened and at a premium of several percent once deposits were shut but withdrawals stayed open, in three assets, under a second reference and in an active market, and the gap closed when the rails returned. Run hourly over 10 months, the method flags ledger failure in 67.7% of rail-cut hours and in no SVB or FTX hour across 9 threshold settings. Sterling and euro rail cuts show only small effects, a pre-registered multi-event study covers token failures, and all findings are descriptive; the ledger analysis came from a disclosed search.

**Suggested keywords:** stablecoins; platform money; exchange ledgers; price feeds and oracles; Web measurement; natural experiment; reproducibility
